stem: What is the average-case time complexity of a lookup in a well-implemented hash table with $n$ keys? $$T(n) = ?$$
explanation: Under uniform hashing with a bounded load factor, expected chain length (or probe count) is $O(1)$.

optionExplanations.A: Correct — the whole point of a hash table.
optionExplanations.C: Only the worst case (all keys collide).

sourceRefs.title: CLRS §11 Hash Tables
sourceRefs.supports: Expected O(1) lookup under simple uniform hashing.

stem: Which of the following comparison-based sorting algorithms have a **worst-case** time complexity of $O(n \log n)$? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Merge sort and heap sort guarantee $O(n \log n)$ in the worst case. Randomised quicksort has expected $O(n \log n)$ but worst-case $O(n^2)$; bubble sort is $O(n^2)$.

optionExplanations.A: Correct — deterministic O(n log n) worst case.
optionExplanations.B: Correct — O(n log n) worst case.
optionExplanations.C: Worst case is O(n^2) even with randomised pivot (very unlikely, but possible).

distractorRationales.D: Confuses one of the classic O(n^2) sorts with an O(n log n) sort.

sourceRefs.title: CLRS §7-8
sourceRefs.supports: Worst-case complexity of quicksort, merge sort, heap sort.

stem: Which data structure gives $O(1)$ push and $O(1)$ pop from **either end**?
explanation: A deque supports amortised $O(1)$ operations at both ends (via a doubly-linked list or a circular buffer).

optionExplanations.A: Only one-end O(1); tail operations become O(n) without an explicit tail pointer.
optionExplanations.D: Insertion / deletion are O(log n) at best.

stem: You solve $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)$ by the master theorem. What is $T(n)$?
explanation: This is case 2 of the master theorem: $a = 2$, $b = 2$, $\log_b a = 1$, $f(n) = O(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b a})$, so $T(n) = \Theta(n \log n)$.

optionExplanations.D: That would correspond to a very different recurrence.
